en.title: United Kingdom: services power, fiscal constraint and the reconstruction of a post-Brexit growth model
en.deck: The UK combines global services, finance, science and defence capabilities with weak productivity, high debt-service costs, post-Brexit trade frictions and an investment challenge spanning housing, energy and regional infrastructure.
en.regime: Post-Brexit capital and productivity reconstruction: global services and institutional flexibility coexist with weak productivity, expensive public debt, regional imbalances and a renewed industrial-energy-security investment cycle.
en.key_risk: Weak productivity and high debt-service costs compress fiscal space before housing, grids, defence and industrial investment raise productive capacity.

pt-BR.title: Reino Unido: potência em serviços, restrição fiscal e reconstrução de um modelo de crescimento pós-Brexit
pt-BR.deck: O Reino Unido combina serviços globais, finanças, ciência e defesa com produtividade fraca, juros elevados da dívida, fricções pós-Brexit e um desafio de investimento em habitação, energia e infraestrutura regional.
pt-BR.regime: Reconstrução pós-Brexit de capital e produtividade: serviços globais e flexibilidade institucional coexistem com produtividade fraca, dívida pública cara, desequilíbrios regionais e novo ciclo industrial-energético-de segurança.
pt-BR.key_risk: Produtividade fraca e juros elevados comprimem espaço fiscal antes que investimentos em habitação, redes, defesa e indústria elevem capacidade produtiva.

selection_rationale: The United Kingdom is explicitly implicated in the existing Europe–Russia–Ukraine conflict-system research but lacked a reusable country-level context. A country dossier is warranted to connect the UK's post-Brexit trade regime, services-export model, productivity problem, fiscal and monetary autonomy, devolution, energy transition, defence-industrial expansion and regional capital allocation.
contrary_evidence: The UK retains globally important finance, professional services, science, universities, aerospace, defence, life sciences and clean-energy capabilities, arguing against a simple post-Brexit decline thesis.
Strong first-half 2026 GDP growth does not by itself resolve the deeper productivity, investment, housing and fiscal constraints; cyclical recovery and structural performance are kept separate.
limitations: ONS labour-market and productivity data are subject to Labour Force Survey quality caveats and revisions.
The latest population estimate is mid-2025 and the latest long-term migration flow is the year ending December 2025.
The March 2026 OBR fiscal forecast predates the July 2026 change of prime minister and is used as an inherited baseline rather than a full current-policy forecast.
Great Britain clean-power metrics exclude Northern Ireland and are not identical to whole-UK energy statistics.
Government industrial, energy and defence targets are policy commitments, not evidence of completed investment or capacity.
